options.a: A possible steering-system defect
options.b: Normal free play for a power-steering truck
options.c: Low tire pressure on the steer axle
options.d: A loose fifth-wheel mounting

distractorExplanations.b: Manuals treat play beyond about 10 degrees (2 inches on a 20-inch wheel) as a defect, even on a truck with power steering.
distractorExplanations.c: Low steer-tire pressure causes hard steering or pulling to one side, not excessive free play at the steering wheel.
distractorExplanations.d: A loose fifth wheel shows as movement between tractor and trailer, not as free play in the steering wheel.

options.a: Tread depth of 3/32 inch on a drive tire
options.b: Exposed fabric or cord in the tread or sidewall
options.c: Mismatched brands of tire on the same axle
options.d: A retreaded tire mounted on a drive or trailer axle

distractorExplanations.a: Non-steer tires need at least 2/32 inch of tread; 3/32 inch on a drive tire is still legal, so it is not an out-of-service defect.
distractorExplanations.c: Different brands are allowed; the real problem is mixing radial and bias-ply tires or mismatched sizes on one axle.
distractorExplanations.d: Retreads are allowed on drive and trailer axles; the restriction is on the front steer wheels of buses.

options.a: Increase engine speed to raise the reading
options.b: Add oil at the next stop and continue if the light goes out
options.c: Stop safely as soon as possible and shut down the engine
options.d: Keep driving if coolant temperature stays in the normal range

distractorExplanations.b: Near-zero oil pressure can destroy the engine within minutes; driving on to the next stop risks seizure, so stop and shut down now.
distractorExplanations.d: Normal coolant temperature says nothing about lubrication; a near-zero oil-pressure reading requires an immediate safe stop.
distractorExplanations.a: “Increase engine speed to raise the reading” is incorrect because near-zero oil pressure can destroy an engine quickly. The driver should make a safe stop, shut down, and have the lubrication problem corrected.

options.a: Mirror adjustment is required on the post-trip report
options.b: Mirrors only need checking each time the trailer is changed
options.c: Mirrors eliminate the need for shoulder checks
options.d: Damaged or misadjusted mirrors leave critical areas unseen

distractorExplanations.a: Mirrors are checked pre-trip because they must work before driving; the post-trip DVIR is not the reason for the inspection.
distractorExplanations.b: Mirrors can be knocked out of adjustment or damaged at any time and are checked on every pre-trip, not just after a trailer swap.
distractorExplanations.c: “Mirrors eliminate the need for shoulder checks” is incorrect because properly mounted and adjusted mirrors are essential for monitoring traffic and blind areas; cracked, loose, or obstructed mirrors compromise safe operation.

options.a: Maintain steering control during hard braking on slippery surfaces
options.b: Shorten stopping distances on loose gravel and fresh snow surfaces
options.c: Prevent every skid even when the driver enters a curve too fast
options.d: Replace the need to maintain safe following distance

distractorExplanations.b: On loose gravel or fresh snow ABS can lengthen stops because locked wheels would build a wedge of material; its benefit is steering control.
distractorExplanations.c: “Prevent every skid even when the driver enters a curve too fast” is incorrect because aBS prevents wheel lockup so the driver can steer while braking hard; it does not guarantee shorter stops on every surface.
distractorExplanations.d: “Replace the need to maintain safe following distance” is incorrect because aBS prevents wheel lockup so the driver can steer while braking hard; it does not guarantee shorter stops on every surface.

options.a: Pressure ratings on the sidewall assume a hot tire
options.b: Heat from driving raises pressure and can mask underinflation
options.c: FMCSA rules allow pressure checks only on cold tires
options.d: Hot tires lose pressure, so a hot reading shows false underinflation

distractorExplanations.a: Sidewall and recommended pressures are cold-inflation figures; that is why checks are made on cool tires, not because they assume hot ones.
distractorExplanations.c: No federal rule bans checking hot tires; cold checks are preferred because heat inflates the reading, not because of a legal limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Heat raises tire pressure rather than lowering it, so a hot reading overstates inflation instead of understating it.

options.a: Normal carbon buildup from a diesel engine at idle
options.b: A clogged diesel particulate filter needing regeneration
options.c: An exhaust leak that may allow fumes to enter the cab
options.d: An oil leak dripping onto the hot exhaust manifold

distractorExplanations.a: Soot at a joint or clamp marks escaping exhaust gas, not harmless idle buildup; the leak must be repaired before operation.
distractorExplanations.b: A DPF problem shows as a dash warning or lost power; soot around one connection points to a leak at that joint.
distractorExplanations.d: Oil on the manifold leaves wet residue, smoke or a burning smell, while dry black soot at a connection marks an exhaust leak.

options.a: Shut off the engine immediately while still in traffic
options.b: Increase speed to force more air through the radiator
options.c: Open the hot radiator cap to check coolant
options.d: Pull off safely, idle to cool if safe, and investigate

distractorExplanations.c: Opening a hot, pressurized radiator can spray scalding coolant; let the system cool before checking the level.
distractorExplanations.a: Immediate shutdown in a travel lane creates a collision hazard; get clear first when possible.
distractorExplanations.b: Higher speed increases load and may worsen overheating.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-ve.explanation: Overheating requires a safe stop and diagnosis (coolant, belts, debris). Stopping in traffic lanes or forcing the engine harder worsens risk. Investigate before continuing.

options.a: Hose condition sets the engine's oil-pressure reading
options.b: Cracks, bulges, or leaks can lead to coolant loss
options.c: Bulging hoses only matter on gasoline engines
options.d: Collapsed hoses show the coolant is properly full

distractorExplanations.a: Coolant hoses carry coolant, not oil; oil pressure depends on the lubrication system, so hoses are checked to prevent overheating.
distractorExplanations.c: Diesel cooling systems use the same pressurized hoses; a bulge or crack can fail and drain coolant on any engine.
distractorExplanations.d: A collapsed or soft hose suggests a leak, failed cap or blockage, not a full system; it is a defect to report.

options.a: Normal warm-up for a turbocharged diesel in cold weather
options.b: A serious lubrication problem that can destroy the engine quickly
options.c: A stuck coolant thermostat that will clear as the engine warms
options.d: Low DEF level, which also triggers an oil-pressure warning

distractorExplanations.a: Oil pressure should rise within seconds of start-up even when cold; staying near zero is a lubrication failure, not warm-up.
distractorExplanations.c: The thermostat controls coolant flow and temperature; it does not affect oil pressure, which comes from the oil pump.
distractorExplanations.d: DEF is an emissions fluid with its own gauge and derate warnings; it has no link to engine oil pressure.

options.a: Suspension wear changes the GVWR stamped on the frame
options.b: Damaged suspension can cause poor control and unsafe ride height
options.c: Suspension checks are needed only after carrying heavy loads
options.d: Suspension defects affect ride comfort but not braking or steering

distractorExplanations.a: GVWR is a manufacturer rating that wear cannot change; damaged suspension is checked because it threatens vehicle control.
distractorExplanations.c: Broken springs, leaking air bags or cracked U-bolts can occur on any trip; suspension is checked on every pre-trip.
distractorExplanations.d: Suspension holds axles in position; a broken spring or shifted axle can affect steering, braking and stability.

options.a: Press harder on the brakes to make up for the fade
options.b: Shift into a higher gear to reduce engine load on the grade
options.c: Move to a safe stopping place and allow the brakes to cool
options.d: Pour water on the hot brake drums to cool them quickly

distractorExplanations.a: More pressure on faded brakes adds heat and can lead to complete brake failure; stop and let them cool.
distractorExplanations.b: A higher gear reduces engine braking and lets speed build faster; a lower gear is needed, then a stop to cool the brakes.
distractorExplanations.d: Dousing hot drums can crack them through thermal shock; let the brakes cool naturally after a safe stop.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-ve.explanation: Burning odor and reduced braking indicate overheated brakes or fade. The driver must stop safely and inspect rather than continue with diminished braking. Inspect the brakes once they have cooled.

options.a: Wipers must work only when rain is forecast for the route
options.b: Clear forward vision is required for safe operation
options.c: They replace the need to inspect mirrors and lights
options.d: Wiper blades are checked for the annual inspection, not pre-trip

distractorExplanations.a: Weather and road spray change without warning; wipers and washers are checked on every pre-trip, not just when rain is forecast.
distractorExplanations.d: Wipers and washers are daily pre-trip items because a failure in rain or spray immediately limits vision.
distractorExplanations.c: “They replace the need to inspect mirrors and lights” is incorrect because impaired visibility is a major crash risk; wipers/washers are essential inspection items.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-ve.explanation: Impaired visibility is a major crash risk; wipers/washers are essential inspection items. A driver must identify safety defects during inspection and keep the vehicle out of service when a defect threatens control. Rain, snow, and road spray all demand working wipers.

options.a: Small power-steering leaks are normal on heavy trucks
options.b: Loss of fluid can reduce steering assistance and control
options.c: The fluid leak can drain the engine's oil supply
options.d: Loss of fluid can disable the air-brake compressor

distractorExplanations.a: Any steering-fluid leak is a defect; continued loss reduces assist and can make the truck hard to steer in an emergency.
distractorExplanations.c: Power-steering fluid is a separate system from engine oil; the danger is losing steering assist, not engine lubrication.
distractorExplanations.d: The air compressor does not use power-steering fluid; the leak threatens steering assist, not the brake air supply.

options.a: One second for each 10 feet of vehicle length at speeds under 40 mph
options.b: One second for each 15 feet of vehicle length at speeds under 40 mph
options.c: One second for each 20 feet of vehicle length at any speed
options.d: A fixed four-second gap, the same as a passenger car

distractorExplanations.b: The manual rule is one second per 10 feet under 40 mph; one second per 15 feet leaves a third less time than required.
distractorExplanations.c: One second per 20 feet halves the manual's minimum and ignores the extra second needed above 40 mph.
distractorExplanations.d: Heavy vehicles need length-based time—one second per 10 feet plus one more above 40 mph—not a fixed car-style gap.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Commercial manuals teach length-based following time (e.g., 1 second per 10 ft under 40 mph) and more space at higher speeds or in poor conditions. Add one more second at speeds above 40 mph.

options.a: Swing left into the adjacent lane before starting the turn
options.b: Swing wide as needed while keeping the rear clear of hazards
options.c: Cut the corner tightly to stay in one lane
options.d: Begin turning early so the trailer follows the tractor's path

distractorExplanations.a: Swinging wide to the left before a right turn invites cars to pass on your right; swing wide as you complete the turn instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Trailers off-track inside the tractor's path; turning early drags the trailer over the curb rather than making it follow.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting tight often curbs the trailer wheels.

options.a: Ice forming under tires below freezing temperatures
options.b: Brakes locking on wet pavement
options.c: Water buildup under tires reducing traction
options.d: Oil residue lifting from pavement in the first rain

distractorExplanations.a: That describes ice or black ice; hydroplaning is tires riding on a film of water, often at speeds above about 30 mph.
distractorExplanations.b: Lockup is a braking skid; hydroplaning occurs when water lifts the tires off the road, even without any braking.
distractorExplanations.d: Oil residue makes early rain slippery, but hydroplaning is water building under the tires so they lose road contact.

options.a: Use steady, light brake pressure all the way down
options.b: Start in a high gear and downshift as speed builds
options.c: Hold speed with the trailer hand valve
options.d: Select a safe low gear before starting down

distractorExplanations.a: Constant light braking overheats and fades the brakes; manuals teach a low gear plus snub braking.
distractorExplanations.b: Downshifting after speed builds is often impossible and risks a missed shift; choose the low gear before the grade.
distractorExplanations.c: The trailer hand valve brakes the trailer alone and can overheat those brakes or cause a skid; it is not for grade speed control.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Choose a gear that holds speed without excessive braking; then use steady or snub braking as trained—not high gear or engine-off coasting. Then use proper (snub) braking technique.

options.a: Increase your following distance ahead and avoid sudden moves
options.b: Brake sharply to force the tailgater to back away
options.c: Reduce the space ahead so the tailgater can pass sooner
options.d: Speed well above the limit until the other vehicle falls behind

distractorExplanations.b: “Brake sharply to force the tailgater to back away” is incorrect because create more cushion ahead so you can brake gradually; aggressive braking or blocking escalates risk.
distractorExplanations.c: “Reduce the space ahead so the tailgater can pass sooner” is incorrect because create more cushion ahead so you can brake gradually; aggressive braking or blocking escalates risk.
distractorExplanations.d: “Speed well above the limit until the other vehicle falls behind” is incorrect because create more cushion ahead so you can brake gradually; aggressive braking or blocking escalates risk.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Create more cushion ahead so you can brake gradually; aggressive braking or blocking escalates risk. The general-knowledge test favors smooth control, adequate space, lower speed, and early hazard recognition. Do not speed up just to please the tailgater.

options.a: Stare into their headlights to judge distance
options.b: Look toward the right edge of your lane until they pass
options.c: Flash your high beams and hold them on until they dim
options.d: Look toward the center line to track the oncoming car

distractorExplanations.c: Holding high beams on blinds the other driver too and raises crash risk; dim yours and look toward the right edge.
distractorExplanations.d: Looking toward the center line keeps the glare in view; the manual says to look to the right side of the road.
distractorExplanations.a: Staring into headlights worsens temporary blindness.

options.a: Whenever driving through heavy rain or fog at normal highway speed
options.b: Instead of using turn signals during lane changes
options.c: When you are moving unusually slowly or stopped as a hazard to traffic
options.d: Continuously in clear weather during ordinary highway travel

distractorExplanations.a: Flashers while moving at normal speed confuse drivers about whether you are stopped; use low-beam headlights instead.
distractorExplanations.b: “Instead of using turn signals during lane changes” is incorrect because flashers warn others of a hazard (breakdown, very slow travel). Misuse can confuse other drivers; follow local/company policy.
distractorExplanations.d: “Continuously in clear weather during ordinary highway travel” is incorrect because flashers warn others of a hazard (breakdown, very slow travel). Misuse can confuse other drivers; follow local/company policy.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Flashers warn others of a hazard (breakdown, very slow travel). Misuse can confuse other drivers; follow local/company policy. Follow company and state rules on flasher use.

options.a: The gap you keep ahead only, measured in seconds of travel
options.b: The extra lane width a wide-turning rig borrows at corners
options.c: The clearance below overpasses that you check before entering
options.d: The open space you maintain around your vehicle to escape hazards

distractorExplanations.a: Following distance is one part; a space cushion also includes space behind, to the sides and overhead.
distractorExplanations.b: Swinging wide is a turning technique; the space cushion is the open area kept around the vehicle at all times.
distractorExplanations.c: Overhead clearance is one part of space management, but the space cushion is the open area kept all around the vehicle.

options.a: Release the brakes to regain rolling traction, then steer
options.b: Press harder on the brakes until the skid stops
options.c: Steer sharply away from the skid before releasing the brakes
options.d: Shift to neutral and keep steady pressure on the brakes

distractorExplanations.b: More pressure keeps the wheels locked; releasing the brakes lets the tires roll and regain steering traction.
distractorExplanations.c: Locked wheels cannot steer, so steering first does nothing; release the brakes first, then steer.
distractorExplanations.d: Neutral removes engine braking and steady pressure keeps the wheels locked; release the brakes to regain traction.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Locked wheels cannot steer; releasing brakes restores rolling contact so you can steer and then brake properly. Reapply the brakes gently as needed.

options.a: Drafting beside a car reduces your truck's wind resistance
options.b: They may change lanes into you without seeing your vehicle
options.c: It blocks your view of the road shoulder on that side
options.d: It forces you to brake harder when traffic ahead slows

distractorExplanations.a: Riding alongside another vehicle gives no meaningful drag benefit; the risk is that its driver cannot see you and merges.
distractorExplanations.c: The concern is the other driver's view, not yours; lingering where they cannot see you invites a lane change into your rig.
distractorExplanations.d: Braking depends on space ahead; the blind-spot problem is that the other driver may merge into you without warning.

options.a: The same following distance as a passenger car
options.b: More following distance because stopping distance is longer
options.c: Less following distance if the truck has ABS and disc brakes
options.d: Less distance because air brakes apply faster than hydraulic

distractorExplanations.c: ABS and disc brakes improve control but do not bring a loaded CMV's stopping distance down to a car's; more space is still needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Air brakes add about half a second of brake lag before full braking; they do not apply faster than hydraulic brakes.
distractorExplanations.a: “The same following distance as a passenger car” is incorrect because greater mass and longer stopping distance require more space ahead than light vehicles.

options.a: Mirrors cover the rear well enough on a straight back
options.b: Blind spots are large; use a helper and get out to look
options.c: Backing toward the blind (right) side is preferred
options.d: Backup alarms make a helper or walk-around unnecessary

distractorExplanations.a: Mirrors leave a large blind area directly behind the trailer; even a straight back needs a get-out-and-look check or helper.
distractorExplanations.c: Manuals prefer backing toward the driver's side, where you can see; blind-side backing is the riskier choice.
distractorExplanations.d: Alarms warn people but do not show you obstacles; a helper or getting out to look is still needed.

options.a: Cool the brake drums so braking improves right afterward
options.b: Wet brakes and reduce braking effectiveness until they dry
options.c: Flood the air tanks and lock the spring brakes
options.d: Cause hydroplaning on the next dry stretch of road

distractorExplanations.a: Water on the linings reduces friction, so braking is weaker until they dry; it is not a cooling benefit.
distractorExplanations.c: Air tanks are a sealed system; deep water affects the brake linings, not reservoir pressure or the spring brakes.
distractorExplanations.d: Hydroplaning needs water on the road surface; the after-effect of a deep crossing is wet, weak brakes.

options.a: Signal, then merge slowly so they can make room
options.b: Avoid lane changes until you confirm the space is clear
options.c: Speed up so they fall behind your trailer, then merge
options.d: Merge once they have been out of the mirror a few seconds

distractorExplanations.a: Signaling does not make the lane clear; wait until you can see the vehicle has left your blind spot.
distractorExplanations.c: Speeding up to clear them still leaves the vehicle unseen and adds speed; wait until you confirm the lane is clear.
distractorExplanations.d: A vehicle out of the mirror may be in the blind spot itself; confirm the space is clear, not just that the mirror is empty.

options.a: To prevent cargo from shifting or falling
options.b: To keep axle weights within legal limits
options.c: To protect the cargo from shipping damage
options.d: To set the shipper's liability for loads

distractorExplanations.b: Axle limits come from weight laws and load placement; securement rules control movement of the load.
distractorExplanations.c: Damage protection is a commercial concern; FMCSA securement rules exist to prevent shifting and falling loads that cause crashes.
distractorExplanations.d: Liability is covered by the bill of lading and contracts; securement rules target road safety from shifting or falling cargo.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-ca.explanation: Securement keeps loads stable under acceleration, braking, and turns so cargo does not spill or destabilize the vehicle. Loose or falling cargo causes crashes and roadway hazards.

options.a: The rated maximum weight of a single vehicle and its load
options.b: The maximum allowable weight of the power unit plus trailer(s) and cargo
options.c: The actual weight of the loaded combination when weighed on a scale
options.d: The maximum weight a single axle may carry on interstate roads

distractorExplanations.a: That is GVWR; GCWR is the rating for the power unit plus its trailer(s) and cargo combined.
distractorExplanations.c: Actual weight is gross combination weight (GCW); GCWR is the manufacturer's maximum rating, not the scale reading.
distractorExplanations.d: Axle limits (20,000 lb on a single axle) are legal weight limits; GCWR is a manufacturer rating for the entire combination.

options.a: Light steering and front-wheel skids on wet roads
options.b: Poor drive-axle traction on slippery winter road surfaces
options.c: Hard steering and possible tire overload / poor handling
options.d: Trailer brake lockup during normal hard stops

distractorExplanations.a: Light steering comes from too little weight on the steer axle; too much weight causes hard steering and tire overload.
distractorExplanations.b: Poor drive traction results from too little weight on the drive axles, not from overloading the steer axle.
distractorExplanations.d: Trailer brake lockup comes from light trailer axles; excess steer-axle weight affects steering effort and front tires.

options.a: It adds traction to the drive axles on slippery road surfaces
options.b: It shifts weight forward and overloads the steer axle
options.c: It increases off-tracking of the trailer at low speed
options.d: It raises the center of gravity and increases rollover risk

distractorExplanations.a: Height does not add traction; a high center of gravity mainly raises rollover risk in curves and sudden turns.
distractorExplanations.b: A tall load raises the center of gravity; steer-axle overload comes from load placed too far forward, not from height.
distractorExplanations.c: Off-tracking depends on wheelbase and trailer length, not load height; high loads mainly raise rollover risk.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-ca.explanation: High CG makes rollovers more likely at the same speed in curves; load low and centered when possible. Cargo must remain within legal ratings and be distributed, contained, and secured against movement in every direction. The risk is greatest in turns.

options.a: Secure tarp edges so wind cannot get under and tear the cover
options.b: Use the tarp as a substitute for required tiedowns
options.c: Leave the front edge loose so air can escape underneath
options.d: Attach the cover only to movable cargo rather than the vehicle

distractorExplanations.b: “Use the tarp as a substitute for required tiedowns” is incorrect because wind can balloon poorly secured tarps; covers must be fastened so they protect cargo without replacing required tiedowns.
distractorExplanations.c: “Leave the front edge loose so air can escape underneath” is incorrect because wind can balloon poorly secured tarps; covers must be fastened so they protect cargo without replacing required tiedowns.
distractorExplanations.d: “Attach the cover only to movable cargo rather than the vehicle” is incorrect because wind can balloon poorly secured tarps; covers must be fastened so they protect cargo without replacing required tiedowns.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-ca.explanation: Wind can balloon poorly secured tarps; covers must be fastened so they protect cargo without replacing required tiedowns. A loose tarp can also unload cargo onto the road.

options.a: The force at which the tiedown breaks during testing
options.b: The maximum load the device is designed to secure
options.c: The cargo weight the trailer can carry
options.d: The minimum tension a ratchet strap must be pulled to

distractorExplanations.a: That is breaking strength; WLL is a lower rated figure for normal service, set well below the break point.
distractorExplanations.c: Trailer capacity is set by GVWR and axle ratings; WLL rates an individual tiedown or securement device.
distractorExplanations.d: WLL is a maximum rated load for normal service, not a minimum tensioning target for straps.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-ca.explanation: WLL is used to ensure aggregate tiedown capacity meets cargo weight requirements under FMCSA securement rules. WLL applies under normal use.

options.a: Set the maximum overall length of trailers on interstate highways
options.b: Make sure each truck's GVWR matches its registration
options.c: Balance braking force between the tractor and trailer
options.d: Protect bridges and roadways by limiting concentrated axle loads

distractorExplanations.a: Length limits come from separate size rules; the bridge formula limits weight by the number and spacing of axles.
distractorExplanations.b: Registration and GVWR are administrative ratings; the bridge formula limits weight on axle groups to protect bridges.
distractorExplanations.c: Axle-spacing rules are about pavement and bridge loading, not brake balance between units.

options.a: To prevent cargo from moving forward, backward, or sideways
options.b: To distribute weight evenly over the axles for legal limits
options.c: To protect cargo surfaces from tiedown strap damage
options.d: To lower the cargo's center of gravity on the trailer deck

distractorExplanations.b: Weight distribution is done by load placement; blocking and bracing restrain cargo against movement in transit.
distractorExplanations.c: Edge protectors guard cargo from straps; blocking and bracing are restraints that keep cargo from moving.
distractorExplanations.d: Blocking and bracing do not change load height; they fill gaps and restrain cargo so it cannot shift.

options.a: Within the first 25 miles, then only at the destination
options.b: Within the first 50 miles and periodically thereafter
options.c: Within the first 100 miles and every 300 miles after
options.d: Within the first 150 miles, then at each duty change

distractorExplanations.a: Federal rules require rechecks every 3 hours or 150 miles after the first check, not just once more at delivery.
distractorExplanations.c: The first check is due within 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles, whichever comes first—not 100 and 300.
distractorExplanations.d: 150 miles is the recheck interval, not the first-check point; the first inspection comes within 50 miles.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-ca.explanation: Federal securement rules require early and periodic inspections because loads can shift. Cargo must remain within legal ratings and be distributed, contained, and secured against movement in every direction. Rechecks follow every 3 hours or 150 miles, whichever comes first.

options.a: Increase traction by loading the drive axles more
options.b: Lower the center of gravity and improve stability
options.c: Reduce the number of tiedowns the cargo requires
options.d: Shorten stopping distance on wet roads

distractorExplanations.a: Axle loading depends on fore-aft position; keeping cargo low and centered mainly lowers the center of gravity.
distractorExplanations.c: Tiedown count is set by cargo length and weight rules; low, centered placement improves stability, not securement count.
distractorExplanations.d: Stopping distance is driven by speed, weight and brakes; load height mainly affects rollover and handling.

options.a: WLL equals the breaking strength printed on the tiedown
options.b: Aggregate WLL of tiedowns must meet required securement strength
options.c: Aggregate WLL must equal at least twice the cargo weight
options.d: The strongest single tiedown sets the WLL for the whole load

distractorExplanations.a: Breaking strength is much higher than WLL; securement calculations use the lower WLL figure.
distractorExplanations.c: The federal rule is aggregate WLL of at least one-half the cargo weight, not twice the cargo weight.
distractorExplanations.d: Aggregate WLL sums the tiedowns; one strong strap does not set the capacity for the entire load.

options.a: Axle overloads can damage roads/bridges and create violations
options.b: Legal GVW makes each axle legal under federal weight rules
options.c: Axle overloads only affect tire wear, not legality
options.d: Poor distribution lowers the GCWR the tractor may pull

distractorExplanations.b: Each axle and axle group has its own limit; a legal gross weight can still put one axle over its limit.
distractorExplanations.c: Overloaded axles are citable violations and can damage roads and bridges; the issue goes well beyond tire wear.
distractorExplanations.d: GCWR is a fixed manufacturer rating; poor distribution creates axle overloads, not a lower rating.

options.a: An open tailgate so loose material can leave gradually
options.b: Adequate covering or containment to prevent cargo loss
options.c: Faster travel so wind carries debris behind the vehicle
options.d: No restraint when the load remains below the side rails

distractorExplanations.a: “An open tailgate so loose material can leave gradually” is incorrect because loose material must be contained so it does not endanger other road users.
distractorExplanations.c: “Faster travel so wind carries debris behind the vehicle” is incorrect because loose material must be contained so it does not endanger other road users.
distractorExplanations.d: “No restraint when the load remains below the side rails” is incorrect because loose material must be contained so it does not endanger other road users.

options.a: Get everyone away, call emergency services, and use proper extinguishing methods
options.b: Spray water briefly, then drive on once the flames are out
options.c: Open the trailer doors to check whether the fire reached the cargo
options.d: Keep driving to the nearest exit ramp so responders can reach you more easily

distractorExplanations.b: Tire fires can rekindle after the flames disappear; driving on risks the fire spreading to the trailer and cargo.
distractorExplanations.c: Opening the doors feeds oxygen to a cargo fire; the manual says keep them closed and call for help.
distractorExplanations.d: Moving the truck with a burning tire spreads the fire to the trailer; stop safely, get people away and call for help.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-em.explanation: Tire fires can rekindle and spread to cargo; evacuate, request help, and use appropriate firefighting guidance. Do not drive on a burning tire.

options.a: To mark where a tow truck should park behind the CMV
options.b: To warn approaching traffic of a stopped vehicle hazard
options.c: To satisfy the rule only on divided highways at night
options.d: To mark the safe zone where passengers should wait outside

distractorExplanations.a: Triangles give approaching drivers advance warning; they are not placed for tow trucks or repair crews.
distractorExplanations.c: Warning devices are required whenever a CMV is stopped on the road or shoulder, day or night, on any highway type.
distractorExplanations.d: Passengers wait well off the road; triangles exist to warn approaching traffic, not to mark a waiting area.

options.a: Shift into neutral to save the engine
options.b: Turn off the engine so the compression slows the truck
options.c: Stay on the road and ride it out to the bottom of the grade
options.d: Look for an escape ramp or safe escape path

distractorExplanations.a: Neutral removes engine braking and you may not get back into gear, leaving no retarding force at all.
distractorExplanations.b: Shutting off the engine can cost power steering and air supply; keep the engine running in a low gear.
distractorExplanations.c: Manuals say to use an escape ramp or escape route if one is available rather than ride out a runaway on the road.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-em.explanation: Escape ramps are designed for runaway vehicles; maintain control, warn others, and use any remaining system carefully—never jump out. Downshift if possible and use any remaining braking carefully.

options.a: Protect the scene, notify authorities, and exchange required information
options.b: Move on once the other driver agrees to settle privately
options.c: Wait in the cab until police arrive before setting out any triangles
options.d: Report the crash to your carrier first, then call police if asked

distractorExplanations.b: Crash duties include notifying police and exchanging required information; a private agreement does not replace them.
distractorExplanations.c: Protecting the scene with flashers and warning devices comes first; waiting for police leaves traffic unwarned.
distractorExplanations.d: Authorities are notified as required at the scene; the carrier call does not replace or delay notifying police.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-em.explanation: Post-crash duties include scene safety, notification, and required reports—without creating new hazards or improper admissions. Help the injured only if trained and it is safe.

options.a: Read dispatch messages while moving if traffic is light
options.b: Set navigation and secure loose items before moving
options.c: Use a hand-held phone only for short calls under one minute
options.d: Look away from the road whenever an alert sounds

distractorExplanations.c: FMCSA bans hand-held phone use while driving a CMV for calls of any length; only hands-free, single-touch use is allowed.
distractorExplanations.a: “Read dispatch messages while moving if traffic is light” is incorrect because preparing devices and cab items before departure keeps attention on driving; tasks that require interaction should wait until the vehicle is safely stopped.
distractorExplanations.d: “Look away from the road whenever an alert sounds” is incorrect because preparing devices and cab items before departure keeps attention on driving; tasks that require interaction should wait until the vehicle is safely stopped.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-em.explanation: Preparing devices and cab items before departure keeps attention on driving; tasks that require interaction should wait until the vehicle is safely stopped. Stop safely for complex tasks.

options.a: A first-aid kit and flares in place of triangles
options.b: Spare fuses and a fire extinguisher, with flashers instead of triangles
options.c: Fire extinguisher and warning devices meeting regulatory specs
options.d: Two warning triangles and a first-aid kit for the driver

distractorExplanations.a: Federal rules require three reflective triangles; flares may supplement them, and a first-aid kit is not a required item.
distractorExplanations.b: Four-way flashers do not replace warning devices; three triangles are required along with the fire extinguisher.
distractorExplanations.d: The rule calls for three warning devices plus a rated fire extinguisher; two triangles and a first-aid kit do not meet it.

options.a: Use flashers and set one triangle 10 feet behind the truck
options.b: Set triangles only if the stop lasts over 10 minutes
options.c: Park without warnings if you will fix it in under an hour
options.d: Use flashers and place triangles at required distances

distractorExplanations.a: One triangle is not enough; the rule calls for three, at 10 and 100 feet behind and 100 feet ahead on a two-way road.
distractorExplanations.b: Warning devices go out as soon as possible and within 10 minutes of stopping, not just for stops longer than that.
distractorExplanations.c: Duration does not remove warning requirements.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-em.explanation: Visibility and advance warning protect you and other road users; never stand in traffic lanes. The driver should protect the scene, preserve vehicle control, warn others, and use the safest available stopping or recovery option. Stay visible and off the travel lanes.

options.a: The vehicle may finish its current trip but must be repaired afterward
options.b: The vehicle/driver may not operate until the violation is corrected
options.c: The driver may drive on but receives a fine and points
options.d: The vehicle may be driven to the nearest repair shop only

distractorExplanations.a: An out-of-service order bars operation immediately; the trip cannot be completed until the violation is corrected.
distractorExplanations.c: OOS is not just a citation; neither vehicle nor driver may operate until the condition is fixed.
distractorExplanations.d: An OOS vehicle may not be driven under its own power before repair; it is fixed on site or towed.

options.a: Brake firmly at once to slow before the truck pulls
options.b: Hold the wheel firmly and ease off the accelerator
options.c: Steer hard toward the shoulder to get off the road fast
options.d: Shift to neutral and coast to the shoulder

distractorExplanations.a: Braking hard after a blowout can make the vehicle pull or skid; stay off the brake until the vehicle slows.
distractorExplanations.c: Abrupt steering after a steer-tire blowout can cause loss of control; hold firmly and steer gently once slowed.
distractorExplanations.d: Neutral removes the drive force that helps stabilize the truck; hold the wheel, ease off and stay in gear.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-em.explanation: Sudden hard braking can worsen loss of control; grip, stabilize, then stop safely. The driver should protect the scene, preserve vehicle control, warn others, and use the safest available stopping or recovery option. Then steer to a safe stop.

options.a: Any at-fault crash, even when no citation is issued
options.b: Serious traffic offenses and certain alcohol/drug violations in a CMV
options.c: A single speeding ticket for 10 mph over the limit in a CMV
options.d: An hours-of-service log violation found at a roadside inspection

distractorExplanations.a: Crashes alone do not trigger disqualification; disqualifying offenses are listed convictions such as DUI or serious violations.
distractorExplanations.c: Excessive speeding is a serious offense at 15 mph or more over the limit, and it takes two serious offenses in 3 years to disqualify.
distractorExplanations.d: HOS violations bring OOS orders and fines, but they are not listed CDL disqualifying offenses under 49 CFR 383.51.

cdl-general-knowledge-readiness-check-em.explanation: Major and serious offenses (and other listed violations) can disqualify a CDL. The driver should protect the scene, preserve vehicle control, warn others, and use the safest available stopping or recovery option. Certain railroad-crossing violations also disqualify.

options.a: Assume trains will yield to highway traffic
options.b: Make sure there is enough room to clear the tracks
options.c: Shift gears while on the tracks to maintain speed
options.d: Follow the vehicle ahead onto the tracks even when traffic is stopped

distractorExplanations.a: “Assume trains will yield to highway traffic” is incorrect because a driver must not enter unless the entire vehicle can clear the tracks; trains cannot stop quickly and a stalled or queued CMV can be trapped.
distractorExplanations.c: “Shift gears while on the tracks to maintain speed” is incorrect because a driver must not enter unless the entire vehicle can clear the tracks; trains cannot stop quickly and a stalled or queued CMV can be trapped.
distractorExplanations.d: “Follow the vehicle ahead onto the tracks even when traffic is stopped” is incorrect because a driver must not enter unless the entire vehicle can clear the tracks; trains cannot stop quickly and a stalled or queued CMV can be trapped.

options.a: Steer into the skid and avoid overcorrecting
options.b: Brake hard and hold the steering wheel rigidly straight
options.c: Accelerate sharply while turning away from the skid
options.d: Apply the parking brake fully before attempting to steer

distractorExplanations.b: “Brake hard and hold the steering wheel rigidly straight” is incorrect because countersteer appropriately and restore traction gradually; abrupt inputs worsen skids.
distractorExplanations.c: “Accelerate sharply while turning away from the skid” is incorrect because countersteer appropriately and restore traction gradually; abrupt inputs worsen skids.
distractorExplanations.d: “Apply the parking brake fully before attempting to steer” is incorrect because countersteer appropriately and restore traction gradually; abrupt inputs worsen skids.
